evidence.claim: The route through Halifax carries an older highway identity: State Route 360 follows the former alignment of U.S. 360.
evidence.quote: SR 360 is the old alignment of US 360 through Danville, eastern Pittsylvania County, and Halifax County, including the latter's county seat of Halifax

evidence.claim: The U.S. highway moved to a course through South Boston, sharing much of that route with U.S. 58.
evidence.quote: before the U.S. Highway was moved to its present course mostly concurrent with US 58 via South Boston.

evidence.claim: Driving east from the Pittsylvania County line, follow Mountain Road through Vernon Hill to Halifax.
evidence.quote: SR 360 becomes Mountain Road as it enters Halifax County, where it passes through Vernon Hill and Mountain Road

evidence.claim: State Route 360 joins Main Street, then continues east as Bethel Road across the Banister.
evidence.quote: The two highways head northeast together to the northern town limit, where US 501 splits northwest toward Lynchburg as L.P. Bailey Memorial Highway and SR 360 heads east as Bethel Road, which crosses the Banister River

evidence.claim: At the junction with U.S. 360 west of Scottsburg, the onward road becomes State Route 344.
evidence.quote: The state highway reaches its eastern terminus at a four-way intersection with US 360 (James D. Hagood Highway) and SR 344 (Scottsburg Road) west of Scottsburg.

evidence.claim: It passes through Scottsburg and ends at the river park.
evidence.quote: SR 344 heads east through the town of Scottsburg to its end in Staunton River State Park

evidence.claim: Mountain Road leads through Vernon Hill into Halifax, where the highway passes the county courthouse before crossing the Banister River below Banister Lake.
evidence.quote: SR 360 intersects SR 349 (Edmunds Boulevard), a very short route on two sides of the Halifax County courthouse

evidence.claim: Mountain Road leads through Vernon Hill into Halifax, where the highway passes the county courthouse before crossing the Banister River below Banister Lake.
evidence.quote: SR 360 heads east as Bethel Road, which crosses the Banister River a short distance south of its impoundment, Banister Lake.

evidence.claim: State Route 360 joins Main Street
evidence.quote: Virginia State Route 360 joins US 501 along North Main Street

evidence.claim: Along State Route 360, the Mountain Road Historic District brings together houses, churches, a parish hall and a Masonic hall from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
evidence.quote: The district includes 22 contributing buildings located along Mountain Road (State Route 360) and consists of two churches, a parish hall, a masonic hall, and a host of private residences dating to the 19th and early 20th centuries.

evidence.claim: Its buildings include the 1828 Masonic Lodge, the 1831 Methodist Church and St. John’s Episcopal Church of 1844.
evidence.quote: Notable buildings include the Masonic Lodge (1828), Methodist Church (1831), St. John's Episcopal Church (1844)

evidence.claim: Dabney Cosby, Jr. designed St. John’s and several earlier houses in the district.
evidence.quote: Several of the earlier dwellings and St. John's Episcopal Church were designed by Dabney Cosby, Jr.

evidence.claim: The district entered the National Register in 1983.
evidence.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1983.

evidence.claim: The courthouse has a road number at its edges: State Route 349, Edmunds Boulevard, runs along two sides of the Halifax County courthouse.
evidence.quote: SR 360 intersects SR 349 (Edmunds Boulevard), a very short route on two sides of the Halifax County courthouse

evidence.claim: Dabney Cosby designed and built the courthouse in 1838–1839.
evidence.quote: It was designed and built in 1838-1839 by Dabney Cosby.

evidence.claim: The two-story brick building has a T-shaped plan and a portico with four Ionic columns.
evidence.quote: It is a two-story, T-shaped brick building in the Federal style. The front facade features a two-story, tetrastyle portico in the Greek Ionic order.

evidence.claim: It belongs to the larger Town of Halifax Court House Historic District, whose buildings extend from the early nineteenth century into the mid-twentieth.
evidence.quote: Resources include government, commercial, residential, religious, educational and industrial buildings that date from the early-19th Century to the mid-20th century.

evidence.claim: That district includes mills as well as government buildings, houses and churches.
evidence.quote: Halifax Roller Mills (1915), Halifax Planing Mill (c. 1920)

evidence.claim: Look for the courthouse’s two-story portico and four Ionic columns.
evidence.quote: The front facade features a two-story, tetrastyle portico in the Greek Ionic order.

evidence.claim: It belongs to the larger Town of Halifax Court House Historic District
evidence.quote: It is located in the Town of Halifax Court House Historic District.

evidence.claim: The park at the meeting of the Dan and Staunton rivers has changed with the water.
evidence.quote: Construction of the park was begun (at the confluence of the Staunton and Dan Rivers) beginning in 1933; Buggs Island Lake was formed in the early 1950s.

evidence.claim: The Civilian Conservation Corps built most of its buildings and facilities, and it opened in 1936 as one of Virginia’s original six state parks.
evidence.quote:
Most of the buildings and facilities of the park were built by the CCC.
In 1936, Staunton River State Park was opened to the public as one of the original six state parks.

evidence.claim: In 1952, completion of the John H. Kerr Dam and formation of Buggs Island Lake flooded part of the park.
evidence.quote: In 1952, with the completion of the John H. Kerr Dam and the formation of Buggs Island Lake, part of the park was flooded.

evidence.claim: The park is an International Dark Sky Park.
evidence.quote: It is an International Dark Sky Park.

evidence.claim: The Staunton is also called the Roanoke River, but locally the name remains Staunton, pronounced “Stanton.”
evidence.quote: Today the river is also known as the Roanoke River; however, locally it is still called the Staunton River (pronounced "Stanton").

evidence.claim: Its historic district includes cabins built in 1934–1936 and picnic shelters from the park’s early years.
evidence.quote: picnic areas including shelters and latrines (1933–1934, 1934–1935), the cabin area and cabins (1934–1936)
